# Part 2 — navigation gotchas


## 1. The checkpoint trap — check this before anything else

Entire's hooks live in `.claude/settings.json` and load **only if the agent session was
launched from inside that directory**. Launch from the parent folder and you get commits
with no checkpoints — silently. `entire doctor` reports green the whole time, because it
inspects the repo's settings file and cannot see where the agent was started from.

Two commits in this repo (`abbf061`, `4a0a219`) have no checkpoint for exactly this reason.

```sh
pwd                     # must be the repo root that holds .claude/settings.json
entire session current  # must NAME a session, not "No active session found"
entire checkpoint list  # after your first commit, must be > 0
```

**A green `doctor` is not proof.** The only proof is a checkpoint count that goes up
after a real commit.

## 2. Verify a checkpoint actually bound — do not assume

The trailer is on the commit itself, so read it from git rather than trusting a tool:

```sh
git log --format="%h %s%n  ckpt: %(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)" -1
```

Audit the whole branch at once:

```sh
git log <branch> ^origin/main --format="%h %s ckpt=%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly)"
```

## 3. `entire checkpoint list` is branch-scoped

It reports `branch <name>` and counts only that branch. Switch branches and the number
changes. That is not data loss — it is a filter. Confirm with `git ls-remote origin`,
which shows the real refs.

## 4. Checkpoints link by SHA, not by branch

Two consequences:

- **Fast-forwarding a branch into another name is safe.** No SHA moves, so nothing breaks.
- **Rewriting history is the thing that destroys them.** `--force`, amend, or rebase after
  push changes SHAs, and every checkpoint pointing at the old ones is orphaned.

Never run `entire session attach --force` on a pushed branch. It amends the last commit
to add a trailer — rewriting published history. Without `--force` the checkpoint is still
created and the trailer is printed for you to paste into a later commit.

**If two early commits lack checkpoints, leave them.** Backfilling breaks the ten that
work to fix the two that do not.

## 5. The checkpoint ref pushes with your branch

`refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` is a separate ref carrying the checkpoint payload.
`git push origin <branch>` pushes it too — you will see:

```
[entire] Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to origin....... done
```

`entire status` tells you when one is pending:

> `1 checkpoint not yet on origin — it syncs with your next 'git push origin'`

## 6. `main` may be protected on the mirror

A direct push is rejected outright:

```
! [remote rejected] pivot-work-order -> main (protected branch)
```

Non-destructive — nothing changes locally. But **find out early, not at 2:55pm.**

Consequence for judging: the web UI's Overview page renders the **default branch**. If
`main` is stale, that page shows an old commit and "No checkpoint activity", which looks
catastrophic and is purely a display artefact. Check the real state:

```sh
git ls-remote origin
```

Then point people at the branch tree URL and the **Sessions** tab, never the repo root.

## 7. Your work may span more than one session

This conversation produced two Entire sessions (`35d4b996`, then `fea6b82a`), apparently

linking one session:

```

2  last stable before noon  9ab0f807a913 -> 90d1939
```

Also: session titles are derived from prompts. A throwaway prompt becomes the session
name a judge sees. Worth renaming before submission if the UI allows it.

## 8. Checkpoint prompts can cross-attribute between concurrent sessions

With two agent sessions in one worktree, a checkpoint created by session A was observed
carrying session B's prompt text. The **commit linkage is correct**; only the prompt
label is misleading. Know this before reading the checkpoint list as a narrative.

## 9. Two agents in one worktree — rules that actually work

- `git pull --rebase origin <branch>` **before** every commit.
- Stage by **explicit path**, never `git add -A`.
- Agree file lanes up front. Disjoint lanes cannot collide.
- Check `stat -f "%Sm" <file>` if you suspect someone is mid-edit — a file written 90
  seconds ago means the other session is live in it.
- A broken build mid-refactor is usually someone else working, not a bug to fix.

For a scratch worktree, adopt the session **before** the first commit or the commits
will not link:

```sh
entire session adopt <session-id> --from /path/to/primary/worktree
```

## 10. Graph commands worth knowing

```sh
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task in one sentence>"
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X          # callers, callees, types, co-change
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json       # semantic diff
entire graph capabilities --json                 # which languages are semantic vs inventory-only
```

- Run `impact` **before** a risky change. After the edit it does not prove the same thing.
- `impact` self-reports `Completeness: degraded for Go` with warnings next to its answer.
  That is the tool naming its own incompleteness — show it, do not hide it.
- Results are **evidence, not an oracle**. Interface dispatch, reflection and generated
  code leave no edge. `impact --symbol Route.Match` on gorilla/mux reports 0 callers even
  though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.

## 11. The standalone binary has no `graph` prefix

Through the plugin it is `entire graph pivot`. A binary built straight from
`./cmd/entire-graph` takes the subcommand directly:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/eg ./cmd/entire-graph    # needs CGO for tree-sitter
/tmp/eg pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --format json    # NOT "/tmp/eg graph pivot"
```

Getting this wrong produces empty output and a confusing JSON parse error downstream.

## 12. Measure from a clean detached build, not the live tree

To reproduce numbers at an old commit without disturbing a worktree someone else is
using:

```sh
git worktree add --detach /path/to/scratch <commit>
cd /path/to/scratch && go build -o ./bin ./cmd/entire-graph
# ... measure ...
git worktree remove --force /path/to/scratch
```

Counts are **file counts**, so they drift as later commits add files. Label a table with
the commit it was measured at, or a judge re-running the command gets different numbers
and stops believing the page.

## 13. Test gotchas in this repo

- `cmd/graph-bench` fails locally: it clones from github and the local git rejects
  `checkout --end-of-options`. **Pre-existing.** Do not try to fix it; do not claim a
  fully green suite.
- `internal/cli` takes ~55-75s. Budget for it before committing.
- If a test fails on ANSI colour codes, check `FORCE_COLOR` in your environment. Some
  tests read ambient colour settings, so they pass in CI and fail on a developer machine.
  Confirm with `env -u FORCE_COLOR go test ./...` before believing you broke something.

## 14. Before you believe any failure is yours

```sh
git stash push -q <your files>
go test ./...            # does it fail at clean HEAD too?
git stash pop -q
```

Thirty seconds, and it separates "I broke it" from "it was already broken".

# PivotMap

## One-sentence summary

`entire graph pivot` answers what survives a requirement that changed after the code was already
written: which files break the new rule, which ones are built on the files that break it, and which
ones can be left alone.

## Problem, intended user and why it matters

A constraint arrives after the work is done. A dependency may no longer touch customer data. An
architecture rule now forbids background workers. A vendor is dropped. The code is already written,
and the developer now has to answer three questions before touching anything:

1. Which code actually violates this?
2. What else breaks if I rip that out?
3. What can I safely leave alone?

Today that is manual archaeology. `git log` shows what changed but not why anyone chose it. Grep finds
the banned import but not the three modules quietly built on top of it. So the developer either
over-reworks — treating the whole area as suspect — or under-reworks and ships a break.

The user is a developer or a coding agent that has just been handed a changed requirement and needs a
defensible plan for what to keep, rework, and drop, in an order they can start executing immediately.

## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential

**Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence.**

The two halves of this problem map onto Entire's two primitives, and neither half is answerable alone:

- **Entire Graph** knows what connects to what. Given a prohibited package it can name every file that
  imports it, and every file that depends on those, with a confidence score and a source line per edge.
  It cannot know why any of it was built.
- **Entire Checkpoints** know why. A checkpoint carries the session that produced a commit — the intent,
  the reasoning, what was rejected. It has no idea what depends on the result.

PivotMap is the join. Graph supplies the blast radius; a checkpoint supplies the intent behind the code
inside that radius and flags which of the affected files this session actually wrote. Remove Graph and
there is no propagation, only grep. Remove checkpoints and the report can still classify, but it loses
the "why was this built this way" that makes a rework plan trustworthy.

## Architecture and main workflow

One new command in this fork, in three files, registered in the existing dispatcher in
`internal/cli/root.go`:

- `internal/cli/pivot.go` — flags, graph load, the three classification rules, propagation, JSON.
- `internal/cli/pivot_roles.go` — file-role classification and the grouped text report.
- `internal/cli/pivot_plan.go` — the `pivot-plan/v1` work order.

```
entire graph pivot --dependency <prohibited package> [--checkpoint <id>] [--depth N]
                   [--exclude-tests] [--format text|json|plan]
```

Pipeline:

1. **Load the graph.** `sem.LoadOrBuildProviderSnapshot` — the same call `impact` uses, so pivot reuses
   the plugin's existing parse and cache rather than building a second index.
2. **Rule 1, direct conflict.** Any file with an `IMPORTS`, `CALLS`, or `CONSTRUCTS` edge reaching the
   prohibited dependency is **INVALIDATED**. This is checkpoint-independent by design: code written
   before Entire was ever enabled still violates a new constraint, and a classifier that could only see
   checkpointed files would silently clear all of it.
3. **Rule 2, propagation.** Breadth-first from the invalidated set over dependency edges. Anything
   reached is **AT-RISK**, recorded with its hop distance. Capped at 2 hops by default.
4. **Rule 3, the rest.** No path to anything invalidated means **SAFE** — but only for languages the
   graph parses semantically. Files in inventory-only languages are reported as **UNREACHED**, because
   calling a file safe when the parser never checked it for relations would be asserting an absence
   nobody verified.
5. **Checkpoint overlay (optional).** `sem.AnalyzeCheckpoint` folds in what a session changed and how
   many dependents each change has, and marks affected files that session wrote with `*`.
6. **Role pass.** Every file is classified **PRODUCTION | TEST | TEST_FIXTURE | GENERATED | VENDOR |
   UNKNOWN** from signals that cannot be argued with: a `vendor/` path segment, a
   `testdata|fixtures|mocks` segment, the `_test.go` suffix, or the `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`
   header the generator itself wrote. The role never changes a verdict — it decides how the finished
   report is grouped and ranked.
7. **Render.** `text` for a person, `json` for the full classification, `plan` for an agent.

`--exclude-tests` (the same path predicate `impact` and `neighbors` use) drops test files *before*
classification rather than filtering them out of the finished report. The difference matters for
propagation, not just for the listing: a test file is not a foundation anything ships on, so a
production file whose only route to invalidated code runs through a test file should come back Safe,
not At-Risk. The count of excluded files is printed, because a file that was never classified is not
a file that came back Safe.

Every verdict prints the edge that produced it — relation type, target, confidence, source line — so a
reader can check the claim rather than trust it.

### Three design decisions worth defending

**The classifier is rules, not a model.** No LLM produces a verdict. The interpretive step — turning a
sentence like "we can't send customer data through Library X" into the package name `libraryx` — stays
outside this binary, and `--dependency` takes the result directly. That is not only a design
preference: `entire graph doctor` asserts `no_egress=true`, and a model call inside the plugin would
make the plugin's own diagnostic lie.

**Propagation is capped.** Unbounded transitive closure marks an entire repository At-Risk, which is
technically true and completely useless. Two hops, with the distance reported per file, keeps the
output a shortlist a person can actually work through.

**Roles rank the report; they never filter it.** The first version of this tool had a real usability
bug, and it was not in the classifier. One shared test helper reaching invalidated code dragged its
whole package along, and the report printed all of it — every file, with its own evidence block. The
verdicts were correct and the output was unusable, because 187 file names that all resolve to one
`go test ./internal/sem` bury the eight production files somebody actually has to open. The fix is not
to drop those files: a deleted result is a result nobody can audit. The fix is to rank them. Test
fallout collapses to one line per package carrying the command that checks it, production work stays
listed file by file with its evidence, and the JSON still carries all 636 files with their roles.

## Entire Graph findings and verification

Run against this repository at commit `934d180` — 634 files, of which the role classifier calls 277
PRODUCTION, 266 TEST and 91 TEST_FIXTURE:

| Run | INVALIDATED | AT-RISK | SAFE | UNREACHED | excluded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--dependency net/http` | 3 | 78 | 468 | 85 | 0 |
| `--dependency net/http --exclude-tests` | **0** | **0** | 204 | 73 | 357 |
| `--dependency os/exec` | 32 | 287 | 230 | 85 | 0 |

```

The four lines are the whole point. Nothing is hidden — the 32 violations are all still violations —
but the reader now knows that eight of them are files to open and 24 are five commands to run. The
187 at-risk test files, which the previous version printed in full, are four lines:

The last line is the honest case: a package with no Go in it is told so rather than handed a command
that would fail.

## The work order: `--format plan`

The JSON report says what every file **is**. That is the right thing to archive and the wrong thing to
hand an agent, because an agent given a classification invents the plan itself — differently each
time, with no way afterwards to tell what it was supposed to have done. `--format plan` states the
work instead, as `pivot-plan/v1`.

Run at `--dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1` against `53ff6bd`: **278 work items — 8 P0,
11 P1, 259 P2**, with 7 required commands, 6 declared blind spots and 6 must-not-claim clauses.

The `plan_id` is deliberately not quoted here. It is a digest over the head commit, the constraint,
the depth, the flags and the counts, so it changes with every commit by design — that is what makes
two plans comparable or provably different. A fixed id printed in prose is stale the moment anything
lands, and a reader who cannot reproduce it has been given a number to distrust. Read it from the run
itself instead:

```sh
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['plan_id'])"
```

**Every classified file becomes exactly one work item**, so nothing falls between the report and the
plan: `INVALIDATED → REPLACE_OR_REMOVE`, `AT-RISK → VERIFY_AFTER_ROOT_FIX`, `SAFE → NO_ACTION`,
`UNREACHED → MANUAL_REVIEW`. Safe files are included deliberately: a file that was analysed and
cleared is a different thing from a file nobody looked at, and only the plan can tell an agent which
one it is holding.

**Priority encodes what blocks what.** P0 is a direct violation in code that ships — nothing
downstream can be verified until it is gone. P1 is a violation in a test, or shipped code standing on
an invalidated foundation. P2 is covered by running a package, or is not a change at all. Items are
sorted before ids are assigned, so reading the plan top to bottom is reading it in execution order.

**The plan id is deterministic** — a digest of head commit, constraint, depth, flags and counts — so
the same question asked twice is recognisably one plan rather than two.

Two parts of the schema exist because of how an *agent* fails rather than how the graph works:

- **`known_blind_spots`** pairs each limitation with its consequence, and is stated *before* the work

  SAFE means no path was found in this snapshot rather than proof of absence.
- **`execution_contract.must_not_claim`** names the likely failure directly. It is not a bad edit — a
  test catches that. It is a confident report of success nobody ran a command to check. The clauses
  forbid claiming the dependency is gone without re-running pivot, claiming tests pass without
  executing them, treating SAFE as proof of absence, and counting an UNREACHED file as resolved. The
  GENERATED and VENDOR clauses appear only when those roles are actually present, so the contract
  stays signal rather than boilerplate.

`validation.required_commands` is where the package collapse becomes executable: `go build ./...`,
one `go test ./pkg` per affected package, and last the exact pivot re-run that proves the invalidated
count reached zero.

One correctness fix came out of building this. Propagation now carries the originating invalidated
file along the walk. At two hops an at-risk item used to report the intermediate neighbour it was
reached through; `root_invalidated` now names the file that actually has to be fixed first, which is
what the plan orders work by — `internal/cli/callsite.go` points at `internal/gitutil/git.go`, not at
whatever it happened to be reached through.

| — | `abbf061` | — | Classifier, propagation, evidence output. **No checkpoint** — see below. |
| — | `4a0a219` | — | `--exclude-tests` applied before classification. **No checkpoint** — see below. |
| `bb0d72d79dbc` | `2ff8446` | Initial understanding and architecture | Checkpoints bind from this worktree. The header keeps depth and index provenance on uncommitted runs, so a reader can tell how far propagation walked and whether the verdict came off a warm cache. |
| `4a14d2327199` | `934d180` | Last stable state before noon | File roles rank the report instead of listing it: 32 direct violations resolve to 8 production files to open by hand and 24 test files collapsed to 5 package commands. |

### The two commits with no checkpoint are the honest part

`abbf061` and `4a0a219` carry no checkpoint, and that is worth stating rather than hiding. Entire's
hooks live in `.claude/settings.json` and load only when the agent session is launched from inside
that directory. Two earlier sessions were launched from the parent folder, never loaded the hooks,
and produced commits with no checkpoint attached — while `entire doctor` reported green throughout,
because it inspects the repository's settings file and cannot see where the agent was started from.

The failure is silent by construction, which is exactly the class of problem this project is about: a
tool reporting healthy is not the same as a tool having checked the thing you care about. The fix was
to verify the binding directly (`entire session current` naming a session, then `entire checkpoint
list` showing a non-zero count against a real commit) rather than trusting the diagnostic. Every
commit from `2ff8446` onward carries a checkpoint, verified that way.

## Setup, run and test instructions

```sh
mise run build          # builds ./entire-graph (needs Go + CGO for tree-sitter)
mise run test           # go test ./...

entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency net/http
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency net/http --checkpoint <id> --format json

# the agent work order
entire graph pivot --repo . --dependency os/exec --exclude-tests --depth 1 --format plan
```

`mise run test` does not come back fully green on every machine: `cmd/graph-bench`'s clone helper
tests fail wherever the local git rejects `checkout --end-of-options`. Those failures reproduce at
`4a0a219`, before any of this work, and are unrelated to pivot — `internal/cli`, which is the only
package this feature touches, passes in full.

## Known limitations and next steps

- **Static analysis cannot see dynamic dispatch.** A call through an interface, reflection, or
  generated code leaves no edge to follow, so a genuinely affected file can be reported Safe. This is a
  property of the underlying parser, not a bug in pivot, and it is the reason the report ends by saying
  Safe means "no path found," not "no path exists." Observed concretely: `impact --symbol Route.Match`
  on `gorilla/mux` reports 0 callers even though `Router.Match` calls it through an interface.
- **Constraint interpretation is out of scope by design.** Pivot takes a package name, not a sentence.
  The natural-language step belongs outside the no-egress boundary.
- **Prohibited-name matching is path-shaped** (exact, or a `pkg/` prefix). A dependency referred to by
  an alias in source is not currently resolved to its canonical package.
- **Test exclusion is path-shaped, not build-tag-shaped.** `--exclude-tests` recognizes conventional
  test paths (`_test.go`, `*.test.*`, a `test/`/`testdata/` directory segment, and the equivalents in
  the other supported languages). A test helper that lives in a normally-named file is still
  classified, and a production file that happens to sit under `testdata/` is still excluded.
- **Next step:** severity beyond the three buckets — an At-Risk file whose only link is a type
  reference is a much smaller job than one that calls an invalidated function on every request path,
  and the graph already carries enough to tell those apart.

**Step 2 in plain language: ask the graph questions *before* touching any code, and save the answers to files.**

content.text:
**That's the money shot, and it's real — not a fixture.**

Five files in our own repo were reported **SAFE** before this change:

```
internal/sem/grammars/csharp/tree_sitter/array.h    E_PARSE_ERROR
internal/sem/grammars/erlang/tree_sitter/array.h    E_PARSE_ERROR
internal/sem/grammars/fsharp/tree_sitter/array.h    E_PARSE_ERROR
internal/sem/grammars/haskell/tree_sitter/array.h   E_PARSE_ERROR
internal/sem/grammars/perl/tree_sitter/array.h      E_PARSE_ERROR
```

PivotMap used to say *"SAFE — no dependency path to invalidated code, leave alone."* The parser had **failed to read those files at all**. The old report presented a parse failure as a clean bill of health, in the exact words the card forbids. It now says UNVERIFIED and names the parser's own error code.

And the CONFIRMED/HEURISTIC split lands where it should:
- `callsite.go → git.go` — `import_resolved` → **CONFIRMED**, no verify line
- `preflight.go → verify.go` — `package` → **HEURISTIC** → *"VERIFY: confirm in source or by test"*

Same repo, same command, both tiers, self-demonstrating. Now the agent-facing plan.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
feat(pivot): grade every edge as confirmed, heuristic or unverified

Noon Curveball, Track 2: the graph is evidence, not an oracle. A repository using
dynamic dispatch, generated code or reflection cannot be fully resolved by static
analysis, and the product must stop presenting what it inferred as what it proved.

THE ASSUMPTION THAT WAS INVALIDATED

Uncertainty was tiered at the LANGUAGE level and nowhere else. UNREACHED told a
reader that an inventory-only language was never analysed for relations, and the
plan declared six blind spots in a header. Both are global statements. Neither
ever reached the file they applied to.

Verified in source before changing anything, not assumed:

  - Confidence was captured into every pivotEdge (pivot.go:428, :476) and read by
    exactly one line in the entire feature -- a Fprintf in pivot_roles.go. Never
    compared, never thresholded, never able to affect a verdict.
  - RelationRecord.Resolution and .WarningCodes -- the graph's own account of HOW
    it knows an edge -- were not copied into pivotEdge at all.
  - Header.Warnings and Header.PartialFailures were copied into the response
    (pivot.go:348, :544) and then consulted by nothing.

So a file the parser had FAILED on could be reported SAFE, described as "no
dependency path to invalidated code, leave alone". Five files in this repository
were: internal/sem/grammars/{csharp,erlang,fsharp,haskell,perl}/tree_sitter/array.h,
each carrying E_PARSE_ERROR. That is a gap in the analysis presented as a finding
about the code, which is precisely what the card forbids.

HOW THE DESIGN CHANGED

Every edge is now graded, keyed on the graph's own resolution vocabulary rather
than an invented threshold. The measured distribution over all 57,791 relations in
this repository is recorded in pivot_evidence.go, because it decided the rules:

  CONFIRMED   import declarations, and calls resolved to a definition
              (exact, import_resolved) at or above a 0.80 floor
  HEURISTIC   inferred -- name_only, package, type_inferred, pattern
  UNVERIFIED  the parser reported a warning or partial failure on the file

Confidence alone could not carry this. 0.80 covers both `IMPORTS name_only` -- an
import statement physically present in the source -- and `CALLS package`, a guess
about where a call landed. Resolution is the axis that separates them. No relation
in this repository reaches confidence 1.00; the highest is 0.95, so a design that
waited for certainty would have graded everything uncertain.

Surfaced to both audiences the card names:

  users   every evidence line leads with its tier and prints the resolution; a
          VERIFY line sits under any file whose evidence is not confirmed; a new
          UNVERIFIED section names the parser's error code per file; the header
          states the evidence mix before the report is read
  agents  work items carry evidence_quality and verification_required as fields
          to branch on; two blind spots (heuristic-edges, unverified-parse) and
          two must_not_claim clauses forbid treating a heuristic edge as fact or
          counting an UNVERIFIED file towards the constraint being satisfied

A file that would have been SAFE but did not parse cleanly is now UNVERIFIED.
A file that did not parse but has a real path to invalidated code stays AT-RISK --
the verdict still says there is a path, because there is one -- and carries its
uncertainty as evidence quality instead.

WHY THE NEW RESULT IS SAFE

Nothing about a clean parse changed. Evidence quality is graded after the verdicts
are final, exactly as roles are, and never moves one.
TestPivotFullyResolvedBehaviourUnchanged pins all six verdicts of the original
fixture and asserts the unverified bucket stays empty and no file asks to be
verified. The full internal/cli suite passes unchanged at 56.071s -- no existing
assertion was modified. The only edit to an existing test is the pivotVerdict
helper, extended to see the new bucket so an unverified file is not mistaken for
an unclassified one.

The direction of every change is towards less certainty, never more: no file moves
from a weaker verdict to a stronger one, and CONFIRMED requires both a structural
resolution and a confidence floor.

TESTS AND FIXTURE

pivot_evidence_test.go adds the partial-analysis fixture the card asks for -- one
file per pattern static analysis loses: an import read from source, a call matched
only by name, generated code carrying a warning, and a file the parser failed on.
Seven tests cover the tier rules directly, both output surfaces, the weakest-edge
rule, and the fully-resolved regression lock.

Verified: go build ./... clean; go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1 ok 56.071s.
cmd/graph-bench still fails on this machine -- the local git rejects
checkout --end-of-options -- which is pre-existing and unrelated. Not a fully
green suite, and not claimed as one.

GRAPH EVIDENCE, CAPTURED BEFORE THE FIRST EDIT

docs/demo/curveball/ holds the search, three impact runs, the neighbors query that
revealed resolution and confidence per edge, capabilities, and pivot run against
itself. Three findings are recorded there rather than in conversation: the
"degraded for Go" completeness note from before noon no longer reproduces (this
repo reports ok with one JSON partial failure); pivot cannot resolve internal
package paths, so --dependency internal/sem returns zero invalidated; and the
installed plugin has no pivot subcommand, so runs use a locally built binary.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

EOF

new = '''## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted

**The constraint.** *Graph is evidence, not an oracle.* A repository using dynamic dispatch,
generated code or reflection cannot be fully resolved by static analysis. The product must not
present incomplete relationships as certain, must identify when analysis may be partial, must offer
a verification path, must keep working unchanged for fully resolved code, and must let **users and
agents** tell apart confirmed structural evidence, heuristic or incomplete evidence, and claims
needing source or test verification.

### The tempting wrong answer

PivotMap already looked compliant. It ships `UNREACHED` for inventory-only languages, it prints
"SAFE means no path was found, not that none exists", and its plan declares six blind spots that
name interface dispatch, reflection and generated code explicitly. The easy response was "we already
did this."

That response is wrong, and the reason is worth stating precisely: **every one of those is a global
statement, and none of them ever reached the file it applied to.** A reader looking at
`pkg/foo.go — SAFE` had no way to connect it to a disclaimer six sections earlier. We had declared
our uncertainty; we had never localised it.

### The assumption that was invalidated

Uncertainty was tiered at the **language** level and nowhere else. It was never tiered at the
**edge** level. Verified in source before changing anything:

- `Confidence` was captured into every `pivotEdge` (`pivot.go:428`, `:476`) and read by exactly one
  line in the whole feature — a `Fprintf` in `pivot_roles.go`. Printed, never consulted.
- `sem.RelationRecord.Resolution` and `.WarningCodes` — the graph's own account of *how* it knows an
  edge — were never copied into `pivotEdge` at all.
- `Header.Warnings` and `Header.PartialFailures` were copied into the response (`:348`, `:544`) and
  then read by nothing.

So these two rendered and behaved identically:

```
IMPORTS os/exec       confidence 0.80  resolution import declaration read from source
CALLS   verify.go     confidence 0.80  resolution package-level guess
```

**The consequence was live in this repository.** Five files were reported SAFE — "no dependency path
to invalidated code, leave alone" — while carrying `E_PARSE_ERROR`:

```
internal/sem/grammars/{csharp,erlang,fsharp,haskell,perl}/tree_sitter/array.h
```

The parser had failed on them. SAFE presented a gap in the analysis as a finding about the code,
which is exactly what the card forbids.

### What changed

Every edge is now graded, keyed on **the graph's own resolution vocabulary** rather than a threshold
we invented. The rules were chosen from a measured distribution over all 57,791 relations in this
repository, recorded in `internal/cli/pivot_evidence.go`:

| Tier | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `CONFIRMED` | import declarations, and calls resolved to a definition (`exact`, `import_resolved`) at or above a 0.80 floor | `IMPORTS internal/gitutil/git.go -> os/exec` |
| `HEURISTIC` | inferred — `name_only`, `package`, `type_inferred`, `pattern` | `CALLS preflight.go -> verify.go (resolution package)` |
| `UNVERIFIED` | the parser reported a warning or partial failure on the file | `array.h`, `E_PARSE_ERROR` |

**Confidence alone could not carry this.** 0.80 covers both `IMPORTS name_only` — an import statement
physically present in the source — and `CALLS package`, a guess about where a call landed. Resolution
is the axis that separates a fact from an inference. And no relation in this repository reaches
confidence 1.00; the highest observed is 0.95, so a design waiting for certainty would have graded
everything uncertain.

Surfaced to both audiences the card names:

```
users   [CONFIRMED] evidence: IMPORTS internal/cli/verify.go -> os/exec (confidence 0.80, resolution name_only)
        [HEURISTIC] evidence: CALLS internal/cli/preflight.go -> internal/cli/verify.go (confidence 0.80, resolution package)
            VERIFY: HEURISTIC evidence — confirm in source or by test before acting on this verdict.

agents  "evidence_quality": "HEURISTIC", "verification_required": true
        known_blind_spots += heuristic-edges, unverified-parse
        must_not_claim    += "Must not treat a HEURISTIC edge as an established fact..."
```

A file that would have been SAFE but did not parse cleanly is now `UNVERIFIED`. A file that did not
parse but *has* a real path to invalidated code stays `AT-RISK` — the verdict still says there is a
path, because there is one — and carries its uncertainty as evidence quality instead.

### Why the new result is safe

Nothing about a clean parse changed. Evidence quality is graded after the verdicts are final,
exactly as roles are, and never moves one. `TestPivotFullyResolvedBehaviourUnchanged` pins all six
verdicts of the original fixture and asserts the unverified bucket stays empty. The full
`internal/cli` suite passes at 56.071s with **no existing assertion modified**.

The direction of every change is towards less certainty, never more: no file moves from a weaker
verdict to a stronger one, and `CONFIRMED` requires both a structural resolution and a confidence
floor. The semantic diff (`docs/demo/curveball/07-semantic-diff.txt`) is entirely additive —
new fields and functions, nothing removed or renamed.

### The fixture for incomplete analysis

`internal/cli/pivot_evidence_test.go` carries a partial-analysis fixture with one file per pattern
static analysis loses: an import read from source, a call matched only by name, generated code
carrying a warning, and a file the parser failed on. Nine tests cover the tier rules directly, both
output surfaces, the weakest-edge rule, and the fully-resolved regression lock.

### Graph evidence, captured before the first edit

Every graph command was run **before** any code changed, and piped to a file rather than described:
`docs/demo/curveball/01-search-evidence-consumers.txt`, three `impact` runs on the verdict maker,
the propagation walker and the renderer, the `neighbors` query that revealed per-edge `resolution`
and `confidence`, `capabilities`, and pivot run against itself.

Three findings are recorded there rather than asserted from memory:

1. The `Completeness: degraded for Go` note from before noon **no longer reproduces** — this
   repository reports `completeness_level: "ok"` for Go with one JSON partial failure. The earlier
   note was carried forward and is stale; it is not repeated.
2. `pivot --dependency internal/sem` returns **0 invalidated**: `prohibitedMatch` does not resolve
   internal package paths. Recorded as a finding about the matcher rather than reported as an empty
   result.
3. The installed plugin has no `pivot` subcommand — the feature exists only in this working tree —
   so all pivot runs use a locally built binary without the `graph` prefix.'''

content.text:
A normal `git diff` shows changed **lines**. A semantic diff shows changed **things** — functions, types, fields — and whether each was added, removed, renamed, or had its signature changed.

Ours came back like this:

```
+ field pivotEdge.Resolution added
+ field pivotFile.EvidenceQuality added
+ function classifyEvidenceTier added
~ type pivotEdge signature changed (11 dependents)
~ function buildPivotResponse body changed (9 dependents)
```

**Every entry is either `+` (something new) or `~` (something existing kept its name but grew).** There is not a single "removed" or "renamed" line in the whole diff.

**Why that matters:** removals and renames are what break callers. If I'd deleted a field or changed a function's parameters, the 11 things depending on `pivotEdge` would each need checking. Adding a field breaks nobody — old code that doesn't know about `Resolution` keeps compiling and behaving identically.

So it's independent evidence for the card's "existing behaviour for fully resolved code must continue to work." The green test suite says behaviour didn't change; the semantic diff says **structurally it couldn't have** — there was nothing removed for anything to trip over. Two different kinds of proof, and the graph produced the second one.

Small nuance so I'm not overstating it: `~ buildPivotResponse body changed` means the *logic* inside did change — that's the actual feature. The point is the *interface* only ever grew.
so why is that ? dhould entire cmds provide those stuffs ? and how did we do the semantic diff - suinge xuitsing enntire smds or pivotmaps cmds ?

**We used an existing Entire command, not PivotMap.** Specifically:

```sh
/tmp/eg diff --base 90d1939 --head HEAD
```

That's `entire graph diff` — a built-in of the plugin, shipped long before this buildathon. PivotMap contributed nothing to it. (I ran it via `/tmp/eg` only because the installed plugin binary is older than our working tree.)

**Why it can do that:** the graph already knows every function, type and field and where each is defined. Diffing two commits is then just comparing two snapshots of that inventory — which entities exist at A, which at B, and whether a signature moved. Line-based `git diff` can't do this because it has no idea what a "field" is; it only sees text.

**"Should Entire commands provide this?"** They already do, and that's exactly why it's the right tool here. The card names **three** kinds of evidence — *relationship*, *impact*, and *semantic diff* — and asks us to identify which parts of our implementation consume each. So we used all three:

| Evidence type | Command | What we used it for |
|---|---|---|
| relationship | `neighbors`, `search` | found where confidence/resolution live |
| impact | `impact` ×3 | blast radius before editing |
| semantic diff | `diff` | proved the change was additive |

The nice property is that the semantic diff is **independent of us**. If I'd written a paragraph claiming "nothing was removed," you'd have to trust me. Instead a tool we didn't write, reading the commits directly, says it. That's the track's own thesis applied to our own work — don't assert, cite.

The one thing worth flagging for the demo: if a judge clones the branch and types `entire graph pivot`, they'll get `unknown command`. one `go test ./pkg` per affected package, and last the exact pivot re-run that proves the invalidated
count reached zero.

One correctness fix came out of building this. Propagation now carries the originating invalidated
file along the walk. At two hops an at-risk item used to report the intermediate neighbour it was
reached through; `root_invalidated` now names the file that actually has to be fixed first, which is
what the plan orders work by — `internal/cli/callsite.go` points at `internal/gitutil/git.go`, not at
whatever it happened to be reached through.

## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted

**The constraint.** *Graph is evidence, not an oracle.* A repository using dynamic dispatch,
generated code or reflection cannot be fully resolved by static analysis. The product must not
present incomplete relationships as certain, must identify when analysis may be partial, must offer
a verification path, must keep working unchanged for fully resolved code, and must let **users and
agents** tell apart confirmed structural evidence, heuristic or incomplete evidence, and claims
needing source or test verification.

### The tempting wrong answer

PivotMap already looked compliant. It ships `UNREACHED` for inventory-only languages, it prints
"SAFE means no path was found, not that none exists", and its plan declares six blind spots that
name interface dispatch, reflection and generated code explicitly. The easy response was "we already
did this."

That response is wrong, and the reason is worth stating precisely: **every one of those is a global
statement, and none of them ever reached the file it applied to.** A reader looking at
`pkg/foo.go — SAFE` had no way to connect it to a disclaimer six sections earlier. We had declared
our uncertainty; we had never localised it.

Pushed `b155201`, ckpt `e16caa8c1de5`. **Everything is committed and pushed.**

---

### Explaining #2 — the `prohibitedMatch` bug

**What happens:** `pivot --dependency internal/sem` returns **0 invalidated** on our own repo, even though most of the repo does depend on `internal/sem`.

**Why.** The matcher (`pivot.go:600`) compares against edge target IDs, which look like:

```
external:import:os/exec                        ← external package
local/entire-graph:Go:internal/sem/search.go:function:Foo   ← internal package
```

It strips an `external:import:` prefix, then tests exact match, `candidate + "/"` prefix, or `:candidate:` / `/candidate:` inside the ID. For `os/exec` the first rule hits. For `internal/sem`, **none do** — the ID contains `:internal/sem/search.go:`, so the segment tests fail (there's a `/search.go` between `internal/sem` and the `:`), and it isn't a bare prefix either.

**Impact:** the tool works for third-party/stdlib constraints ("drop this vendor", "no `os/exec`") — the actual use case. It silently fails for internal architecture rules ("nothing outside the API layer may touch `internal/sem`"), which is a *very* plausible constraint.

**Why it's ugly:** it returns 0 rather than erroring. An empty result reads as "you're compliant" when it means "I couldn't parse your question." That's the same class of bug we just fixed — a gap presented as a finding.

**Fix:** add a path-segment test — match if the target's file path starts with `candidate + "/"`. Roughly 5 lines plus tests, ~20 min.

**My recommendation: don't.** It touches `buildPivotResponse`'s hot path, we're green and pushed, and it's already documented as a known finding in `docs/demo/curveball/PLAN.md`. A found-and-documented bug reads as rigour; a rushed fix that breaks the classifier at 14:30 does not.

Your call.

```
scripts/pivot-loop.sh

  2. executor   fresh agent, plan as its brief   (the existing cold-agent step)

## Reward hacking and specification gaming

### The uncomfortable fact

If an agent can edit the same working tree, tests, verifier configuration, test runner, environment, repository history, or score artifact that determines reward, then “tests passed” is not necessarily evidence that the task was solved.

This is not theoretical. Recent benchmark-security analysis reported agents or exploit strategies bypassing evaluation pipelines by altering test behavior, parsers, configuration, binaries, files exposed to the evaluator, or environments rather than solving the stated task. The exact details vary by benchmark and must be treated as a warning about harness design, not merely a benchmark-specific issue. [rdi.berkeley](https://rdi.berkeley.edu/blog/trustworthy-benchmarks/)

SWE-bench+ analyzed SWE-bench and reported that 32.67% of successful patches had solution leakage from issue descriptions/comments, while 31.08% of passed patches were suspicious because weak tests did not adequately establish correctness. It also describes SWE-bench Verified as a 500-instance human-verified subset with clearer problems and stronger tests. [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.06992v2)

### Threat model

| Attack | Why it passes a naïve verifier | Countermeasure |
|---|---|---|
| Delete failing tests | No failing test remains | Run tests from a trusted baseline checkout; protect test paths; diff test deletion/addition; hidden tests |
| Add `skip`, suppression, or `xfail` | Findings disappear without remediation | Detect added suppression syntax; forbid suppression changes; allow explicit reviewer-approved exceptions only |
| Stub a function | Surface is removed, intended behavior is not restored | Behavioral tests, API snapshots, property tests, hidden regression tests |
| Remove code rather than repair it | Violation count falls to zero | Require retained exports/behavioral invariants; diff-based deletion budget; human approval for destructive changes |
| Change analyzer config/scope | Finding is no longer measured | Contract and analyzer config supplied outside agent workspace; hash/pin inputs; verify in clean checkout |
| Modify test runner/parser | Runner reports success falsely | Use trusted container/image; separate evaluator host; immutable binaries; attest execution |
| Alter baseline artifacts | “No regression” comparison becomes meaningless | Baseline generated before agent begins; content-addressed and signed |
| Read answer from Git history/web | Benchmark measures retrieval, not repair | Strip future history; restrict egress when the claimed capability is independent diagnosis; use private/held-out tasks |
| Prompt-inject LLM judge | Judge changes rubric or leaks score logic | Never use an LLM judge as sole authority; isolate untrusted content; structured judge inputs; deterministic checks first |
| Commit only selected files / exploit diff scope | Hidden changes evade checker | Verify whole tree and commit range; use clean checkout of agent commit; record `git diff --name-status` |

### What actually works

1. **Run verification from a clean checkout of the candidate commit.**
   The verifier must not use the agent’s live process state, local aliases, modified PATH, shell functions, temporary files, or uncommitted changes.

2. **Keep authoritative contract and evaluator outside the agent write set.**
   The agent can receive a read-only copy. The CI/verifier obtains the authority version from a trusted ref, protected branch, signed artifact store, or an orchestration service.

3. **Hash all critical inputs.**
   Record hashes for:
   - contract;
   - analyzer binary/container digest;
   - baseline report;
   - test command definitions;
   - lockfiles/toolchain;
   - candidate commit;
   - verifier result bundle.

4. **Use a trusted execution environment.**
   Use a pinned container/image or CI runner. Do not accept an agent-provided verifier binary, shell initialization, or generated test runner.

5. **Protect verifier-critical paths.**
   Make contract, workflow, scripts, analyzer configuration, test harness, score parser, and baseline data protected. Any change should force `CANNOT_VERIFY` or human approval.

6. **Use hidden or held-out checks where appropriate.**
   Hidden checks are useful for evaluation and high-risk enforcement, but do not use secrecy as your only defense. The visible checks must still be structurally sound.

7. **Add anti-trivialization invariants.**
   For example:
   - public API symbol set must not shrink unless explicitly allowed;
   - target test files cannot be deleted;
   - no new skip/suppressions;
   - changed production files must preserve package build;
   - expected endpoints or behavior snapshots remain present.

The plan already told an agent what it **must not claim**. It never said what it **must not do**. So an agent could delete the file, hit zero, and claim nothing false.

# Research Prompt

Turn a topic into a single, self-contained prompt the user can paste into an external
AI search tool (Google AI Mode, Perplexity, ChatGPT with browsing) to build a
categorized knowledge base of the best resources on that topic.

## Inputs

1. **Topic** (required) — passed as the skill argument, e.g. "Lethal Trifecta".
2. **Focus notes** (optional) — anything after the topic: audience level, sub-areas to
   emphasize, a time range, or preferred source types.
3. **Conversation context** — if the topic was being discussed, use that to sharpen the
   prompt (but the generated prompt must be fully self-contained: the external AI has
   zero context from this conversation).

## Workflow

### Step 1: Frame the topic
Restate the topic precisely. If it is ambiguous, pick the most likely interpretation
based on conversation context and state that interpretation inside the generated prompt
so the external AI does not drift.

### Step 2: Generate the research prompt
Produce ONE fenced code block containing the full prompt. It must:

- Define the topic and (briefly) why it matters, so the external AI scopes correctly.
- Ask for a **categorized** list of resources using these buckets (drop any that do not
  apply, add topic-specific ones as needed):
  1. **Primary / original sources** — the canonical post, paper, or announcement that
     coined or defined the concept, plus its author.
  2. **Official documentation & vendor notes** — guidance from the orgs/companies
     directly involved.
  3. **In-depth analysis & blogs** — high-signal write-ups, critiques, follow-ups.
  4. **Videos & talks** — conference talks, interviews, explainers.
  5. **Academic / research papers** — peer-reviewed or arXiv work.
  6. **Tools, code & demos** — repos, frameworks, PoCs.
  7. **Discussions** — notable threads (HN, Reddit, X/Twitter) that added insight.
- For EACH resource request: title, author/source, URL, publication date, and a
  one-line note on why it matters. Ask it to flag the single best starting point.
- Demand authority and recency: prefer primary and recent sources, note when something
  is outdated or superseded, and avoid SEO filler / content farms.
- Ask it to surface differing viewpoints and known criticisms, not just consensus.
- End by asking for 3-5 follow-up sub-topics worth researching next.
- Tell it to return real, verifiable URLs only and to say so explicitly if it is unsure
  a link is correct (no fabricated links).

### Step 3: Output
- Print a one-line summary of what the prompt will fetch.
- Then print the prompt inside a single code block, ready to copy.
- Do not add commentary inside the code block.
- Copy the prompt to the clipboard so the user can paste immediately. On macOS, pipe the
  exact prompt text to `pbcopy` (use a heredoc to preserve formatting), then confirm with
  a short line like "Copied to clipboard." If `pbcopy` is unavailable, skip silently.

## Style notes
- The generated prompt is self-contained; never reference "this conversation".
- Keep it tight and skimmable; the external AI should not have to guess intent.
- Adapt buckets to the topic (e.g., a security topic should ask for CVEs, advisories,
  and threat write-ups; a library topic should ask for changelogs and migration guides).

**Single best starting point:** study Berkeley RDI’s *How We Broke Top AI Agent Benchmarks* alongside the A2A and MCP specifications, then design your pipeline around one rule: **the agent environment must be unable to alter or influence the verifier environment, verifier configuration, baselines, or scoring artifacts.** The RDI work makes the core failure mode concrete—shared agent/evaluator state allows “passing” without solving—and A2A/MCP clarify where machine-readable work orders and tool access belong. [rdi.berkeley](https://rdi.berkeley.edu/blog/trustworthy-benchmarks-cont/)

The practical architecture is: capture agent context as immutable provenance; hand off typed work-order artifacts; execute in a constrained branch/sandbox; verify from a clean, separately controlled checkout; publish structured results to the PR. Do not use an LLM judge as the merge authority for code correctness or policy compliance.

## Recommended architecture

### Delivery pipeline

```text
Agent session / decision context
  ├─ transcript/checkpoint reference
  ├─ work-order JSON
  ├─ source graph snapshot
  └─ baseline verification report
                 │
                 ▼
External coding agent execution
  ├─ bounded writable checkout
  ├─ least-privilege token
  ├─ no access to verifier authority
  └─ commit / draft PR
                 │
                 ▼
Independent verifier
  ├─ clean checkout of candidate SHA
  ├─ trusted contract from protected base ref/artifact
  ├─ pinned analyzer/test image
  ├─ immutable baseline
  ├─ deterministic re-analysis
  ├─ build/typecheck/tests/policy checks
  └─ path-integrity / anti-trivialization checks
                 │
                 ▼
PR evidence
  ├─ SARIF findings
  ├─ JSON verification report
  ├─ source-linked evidence
  ├─ OTel trace links
  └─ PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL / CANNOT_VERIFY
```

### Four durable artifacts

| Artifact | Producer | Consumer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `work-order/v1` | Analyzer/planner agent or deterministic CLI | Coding agent | Bounded remediation task with paths, evidence, allowed scope, acceptance checks |
| `verification-contract/v1` | Developer/policy owner | Independent verifier | Defines acceptance criteria, protected paths, timeouts, baseline semantics, and unknown-state handling |
| `verification-result/v1` | Independent verifier | PR/CI/reviewer/next agent | Exact measured outcome, command results, evidence, and unresolved risks |
| `provenance/v1` | Session recorder / CI | Reviewer/auditor | Links task, prompt, transcript/checkpoint, graph snapshot, commit SHA, contract hash, and verifier image |

A2A can carry or reference the work order between independent agents, but do not confuse A2A with a security boundary. A2A standardizes peer-agent discovery, task exchange, and interaction; MCP standardizes an agent’s use of tools/data/resources. Neither protocol by itself prevents an executor from gaming a verifier. [a2a-protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/)

### Recommended protocol split

| Need | Best protocol or format | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Agent uses your local graph CLI | MCP, local stdio transport | Tool invocation contract; keep no-egress CLI local |
| Planner hands bounded task to executor | Versioned JSON artifact, optionally transported through A2A | Durable, auditable, easy to validate and attach to a PR |
| Static-analysis findings posted to PR/security UI | SARIF | Standard interchange for source-linked analysis findings |
| Code symbol graph/index interchange | SCIP | Language-agnostic indexing for definitions, references, implementations |
| IDE navigation/editor integration | LSP | Editor ↔ language-server protocol, not an agent delegation protocol |
| Agent/session/tool observability | OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions | Standardizes trace/span attributes, though agent conventions remain in development |
| CI status and merge gate | GitHub Actions/status checks/rulesets | Existing authorization and PR governance surface |
| Policy decision | Verification contract + OPA/Rego or named deterministic checks | Explicit, auditable acceptance criteria; avoid LLM-only judgment |

### The central criticism

The strongest critique of agent-in-CI designs is not “agents are bad.” It is that they are often inserted into privileged CI environments before teams establish:

- immutable acceptance criteria;
- separation between executor and evaluator;
- least-privilege credentials;
- clean-checkout verification;
- protected workflow/policy files;
- hidden or independent checks for high-risk cases;
- evidence that the task was solved, not merely that a metric moved.

The Berkeley RDI work reports that sharing an environment between agent and evaluator was a pervasive exploit path across multiple benchmark systems. Its direct recommendation—run evaluation outside the agent’s container, make evaluator dependencies read-only, keep reference/evaluation metadata inaccessible, and adversarially test the evaluator—is directly applicable to CI. ### Research implications

1. **Test passing is necessary, not sufficient.** SWE-bench+ and reward-hackability research both indicate that weak tests and leaked answers can make benchmark success unreliable. [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.06992v2)

2. **Independent measurement matters more than agent introspection.** Compiler, sanitizer, static-analysis, and formal methods feedback can improve repair, but the verifier must be insulated from the patch-producing agent. [pure.manchester.ac](https://pure.manchester.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/319587217/2405.08848v1.pdf)

3. **LLM-as-judge has a narrow role.** It can triage, summarize, rank candidate patches, or assess natural-language quality. It is not defensible as the sole merge-blocking verifier for a dependency prohibition, security invariant, regression claim, or source-graph property.

4. **Multi-agent orchestration must earn its cost.** A planner→executor split can help when the planner creates a reusable bounded artifact and the executor has different tools/context. A conversational supervisor layer usually adds latency, ambiguity, and state-management failure modes without automatically increasing reliability. [iclr](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/33314)

## How ours would be used

A developer is in Claude Code or Cursor, on some repo. Constraint lands: *"we're dropping `os/exec`."*

**Today** they'd have to know our CLI exists, know the flags, and read 300 lines of text output.

**With the MCP server**, the agent already in their editor just calls it:

```
Agent → tool: pivot(dependency="os/exec", exclude_tests=true, depth=1)
     ← 46 invalidated, 78 at-risk, 48 unverified
       evidence: 52 CONFIRMED, 71 HEURISTIC
       work items with evidence_quality + verification_required
```

The agent now knows **which of its own findings it may act on and which need a source read** — because `evidence_quality` is a field, not prose.

It fixes the P0 items. Then:

```
Agent → tool: pivot_verify(before_plan, range="HEAD~1..HEAD")
     ← FAIL: files_must_still_exist — regexp.go no longer tracked
```

**The agent cannot certify its own work.** The referee is deterministic code called over a standard protocol.

---

That's the pitch: `entire mcp` exposes *status*; ours exposes *analysis and verification*. Same protocol, complementary surface.

46 invalidated, 78 at-risk, 48 unverified

# Research Prompt

Turn a topic into a single, self-contained prompt the user can paste into an external
AI search tool (Google AI Mode, Perplexity, ChatGPT with browsing) to build a
categorized knowledge base of the best resources on that topic.

## Inputs

1. **Topic** (required) — passed as the skill argument, e.g. "Lethal Trifecta".
2. **Focus notes** (optional) — anything after the topic: audience level, sub-areas to
   emphasize, a time range, or preferred source types.
3. **Conversation context** — if the topic was being discussed, use that to sharpen the
   prompt (but the generated prompt must be fully self-contained: the external AI has
   zero context from this conversation).

## Workflow

### Step 1: Frame the topic
Restate the topic precisely. If it is ambiguous, pick the most likely interpretation
based on conversation context and state that interpretation inside the generated prompt
so the external AI does not drift.

### Step 2: Generate the research prompt
Produce ONE fenced code block containing the full prompt. It must:

- Define the topic and (briefly) why it matters, so the external AI scopes correctly.
- Ask for a **categorized** list of resources using these buckets (drop any that do not
  apply, add topic-specific ones as needed):
  1. **Primary / original sources** — the canonical post, paper, or announcement that
     coined or defined the concept, plus its author.
  2. **Official documentation & vendor notes** — guidance from the orgs/companies
     directly involved.
  3. **In-depth analysis & blogs** — high-signal write-ups, critiques, follow-ups.
  4. **Videos & talks** — conference talks, interviews, explainers.
  5. **Academic / research papers** — peer-reviewed or arXiv work.
  6. **Tools, code & demos** — repos, frameworks, PoCs.
  7. **Discussions** — notable threads (HN, Reddit, X/Twitter) that added insight.
- For EACH resource request: title, author/source, URL, publication date, and a
  one-line note on why it matters. Ask it to flag the single best starting point.
- Demand authority and recency: prefer primary and recent sources, note when something
  is outdated or superseded, and avoid SEO filler / content farms.
- Ask it to surface differing viewpoints and known criticisms, not just consensus.
- End by asking for 3-5 follow-up sub-topics worth researching next.
- Tell it to return real, verifiable URLs only and to say so explicitly if it is unsure
  a link is correct (no fabricated links).

### Step 3: Output
- Print a one-line summary of what the prompt will fetch.
- Then print the prompt inside a single code block, ready to copy.
- Do not add commentary inside the code block.
- Copy the prompt to the clipboard so the user can paste immediately. On macOS, pipe the
  exact prompt text to `pbcopy` (use a heredoc to preserve formatting), then confirm with
  a short line like "Copied to clipboard." If `pbcopy` is unavailable, skip silently.

## Style notes
- The generated prompt is self-contained; never reference "this conversation".
- Keep it tight and skimmable; the external AI should not have to guess intent.
- Adapt buckets to the topic (e.g., a security topic should ask for CVEs, advisories,
  and threat write-ups; a library topic should ask for changelogs and migration guides).

A pivot is the hard case for an agent, and the reason is not the editing. It is that
nobody can say when it is finished. "Remove this dependency" has no natural stopping
condition an agent can check itself against, so the work either stops early or runs on
confidently past the point where it was still right.

PivotMap ships the three pieces a developer needs to put a harness around that work, and
they are deliberately separable — take one, take all three:

| Piece | What it is | What it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pivot --format plan` | a bounded work order: one item per file, priority, evidence, and how well that evidence is known | an agent inventing its own plan, differently each run, with no way afterwards to tell what it was supposed to have done |
| `validation.invariants` | acceptance criteria as **data** — files that must still exist, a deletion budget, flags that must match, and an explicit list of what cannot be checked mechanically | "looks right to me" |
| `scripts/pivot-verify.py` | a deterministic referee: no model, no network. `PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL / CANNOT_VERIFY` | the agent grading its own homework |

The loop is producer → executor → referee, and the referee is code rather than a model on
purpose. An LLM judge would move the trust problem rather than solve it, and it can be
argued with. `files_must_still_exist` cannot.

What that buys a developer on a genuinely hard migration: a scope the agent did not choose
for itself, a stopping condition it cannot satisfy by deleting the problem, and a verdict
that distinguishes "this is wrong" from "I could not check this". The three verdicts in
[Closing the loop](#closing-the-loop-a-verifier-with-no-model-in-it) are that claim tested
rather than asserted — including the case where the agent deletes the file, the original
check certifies it, and the harness catches it anyway.

**What it is not.** This is not a complete verification harness, and the difference is
worth being exact about. There is no sandbox, no pinned analyzer image, no signed
baseline, and no protected-path enforcement — a determined agent with write access to the
verifier can still defeat it. What is here is the analysis half: the work order, the
acceptance criteria, and a referee that runs from a clean checkout. The isolation half is
a CI concern and is named in [Known limitations](#known-limitations-and-next-steps) rather
than implied.

## Practical verdict

A planner → executor → deterministic verifier workflow is genuinely valuable when each role owns a different artifact:

- Planner/analyzer owns **evidence and bounded scope**.
- Executor owns **the candidate patch**.
- Verifier owns **measurement and final status**.
- CI/PR system owns **authority and merge policy**.
- Observability owns **traceability**, not acceptance.

Do not build a chatty multi-agent swarm. Build a small artifact pipeline with strict schemas, clean environments, and protected policy authority. Add A2A only when independently deployed agents need discovery/task lifecycle; add MCP when agents need a standardized interface to your graph/checkpoint tools; add SARIF, SCIP, LSP, and OpenTelemetry as adapters for existing developer surfaces.

1. **Verifier attestation and provenance:** Research SLSA, Sigstore/cosign, OCI image digests, and in-toto to bind a verification result to the exact contract, analyzer, environment, and commit.

2. **GitHub Check Runs and SARIF integration:** Map your `verification-result/v1` and graph evidence into PR annotations, required checks, code-scanning alerts, and developer-readable summaries.

3. **A2A task/artifact mapping:** Compare your proposed `work-order/v1` against A2A Task, Message, and Artifact types to decide whether native A2A adds real value over Git/JSON artifacts.

4. **Adversarial verifier testing:** Build null-agent and exploit-agent test suites that attempt test deletion, suppression insertion, analyzer weakening, config mutation, baseline substitution, and CI workflow modification.

## Direct answer

**The single cheapest integration is: write the work order to a file, then have a second local coding agent read that file and execute it in a fresh session.** No A2A, MCP server, GitHub App, or paid plan is required. Add a GitHub Actions PR comment afterward if you want visible evidence for humans.

Realistically:

- **30–60 minutes:** generate `work-order.json` plus a deterministic agent prompt wrapper.
- **1–2 hours:** add a GitHub Action that runs the analyzer and posts a compact PR comment with the work-order artifact.
- **Half day or more:** SARIF conversion, custom MCP server, remote A2A deployment, or autonomous issue/PR orchestration.

The cheapest “real multi-agent” workflow is therefore:

```text
Analyzer / planner agent or deterministic CLI
        ↓ writes
.entire/work-orders/<run-id>.json
        ↓ read by
Fresh executor agent session
        ↓ commits
Independent deterministic verifier reruns CLI
```

That is genuinely multi-agent because one component produces a machine-readable bounded task and a different agent executes it. It is also more reliable than trying to make agents converse through an emerging protocol.

## Best options

| Option | Cost reality | Least glue? | Right when | Honest effort |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| Local JSON artifact → second coding agent | Free if you already have an agent CLI/account | **Yes** | You want a planner/executor split today | 30–60 min |
| GitHub Actions → PR comment + artifact | Free for public repos; private-repo Actions consumption depends on GitHub plan/included minutes | High | Human review and visibility matter | 1–2 hrs |
| GitHub Issues from work order | Free GitHub feature | Medium | Work orders should become backlog items, not immediate code actions | 1–2 hrs |
| SARIF upload to GitHub Code Scanning | Free for public GitHub.com repositories; private/internal code scanning requires GitHub Code Security entitlement | Medium | Your output is static-analysis findings that humans should triage in Security/PR UI | 2–5 hrs |
| MCP server | Open protocol and local servers are free; model client may cost money | Medium–low | A coding agent needs live query access to your CLI, not merely one JSON plan | 3–8 hrs |
| A2A service | Spec is free; running remote agents/models is not necessarily free | Low today | Independently hosted agents need discovery, remote task lifecycle, streaming, or artifacts | 1–3 days |

## 1. What can consume your JSON work order?

### A. GitHub Actions + PR comment

**Best free developer-facing integration.** It does not make the executor agent autonomous by itself, but it turns your analysis into a visible PR review artifact with minimal infrastructure.

Use it when:

- A developer needs to see `INVALIDATED`, `AT-RISK`, and `UNREACHED` results in the pull request.
- You want a durable link between code change and deterministic evidence.
- You want to upload the raw JSON as an artifact for a second agent or human to download.
- You want your CI to rerun analysis after the executor commits.

GitHub Actions can use `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions such as `issues: write` for comments and `pull-requests: write` for PR-level actions. GitHub documents these permissions explicitly. [docs.github](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-server@3.8/actions/using-jobs/assigning-permissions-to-jobs)

### Minimal workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pivot-work-order.yml
name: Pivot work order

on:
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  issues: write

jobs:
  pivot:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run PivotMap
        run: |
          entire graph pivot \
            --dependency os/exec \
            --depth 2 \
            --format json \
            > work-order.json

      - name: Upload work order
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: pivot-work-order
          path: work-order.json

      - name: Render compact PR summary
        id: summary
        run: |
          python3 - <<'PY' > pr-comment.md
          import json
          d = json.load(open("work-order.json"))
          s = d.get("summary", d)
          print("## PivotMap work order")
          print("")
          print(f"- Direct violations: **{s.get('invalidated', 'unknown')}**")
          print(f"- At-risk files: {s.get('at_risk', 'unknown')}")
          print(f"- Unreached files: {s.get('unreached', 'unknown')}")
          print("")
          print("Raw `work-order.json` is attached as a workflow artifact.")
          print("")
          print("> `SAFE` means no path was detected in this graph snapshot; it is not proof of absence through interfaces, reflection, generated code, or unsupported parsers.")
          PY

      - name: Post or update PR comment
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require("fs");
            const body = fs.readFileSync("pr-comment.md", "utf8");
            const marker = "<!-- pivot-work-order -->";
            const comment = `${marker}\n${body}`;

            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const issue_number = context.issue.number;

            const comments = await github.rest.issues.listComments({
              owner, repo, issue_number
            });

            const existing = comments.data.find(
              c => c.user.type === "Bot" && c.body.includes(marker)
            );

            if (existing) {
              await github.rest.issues.updateComment({
                owner, repo, comment_id: existing.id, body: comment
              });
            } else {
              await github.rest.issues.createComment({
                owner, repo, issue_number, body: comment
              });
            }
```

### Permissions

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  issues: write
```

A PR is represented through GitHub’s issues model for many REST operations, so comment workflows commonly need `issues: write`; GitHub’s REST docs cover issue/PR comment permissions. [docs.github](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/issues/comments)
